    Results
    T98G and U87 MG are both glioblastoma cells, yet they exhibit significant nanostructural and functional 
    differences that underscore the complexity and heterogeneity of glioblastomas. While both cell lines originate 
    from the same aggressive brain tumor in different patients, their distinct behaviors can be attributed to differences 
    in surface characteristics and cytoskeletal architecture. Moreover, these changes in cells are also correlated to 
    their biomechanical properties, such as nanomechanical and viscoelastic properties. However, the exploration 
    of GBM cell lines: T98G and U87 MG can shed light on the inter-patient and intra-tumoral heterogeneities of 
    these cells and their potential implications in invasiveness and malignancy.
    Structural and quantitative analysis of actin filaments
    The actin cytoskeleton provides cell shape and mechanical stability and regulates intracellular trafficking as well 
    as cell migration and invasion36. Actin filaments in GBM cells are a remodeled dynamic network that influences 
    cellular behavior, stiffness, and metastatic potential. The architecture of the cytoskeleton must be understood 
    as actin organization changes are related to tumor progression, therapy resistance, and nanoscale mechanical 
    properties11. The mechanical properties of cancer cells are also strongly influenced by cytoskeletal structure. It 
    has been found that malignant cells are softer than normal cells and hence more deformable, which facilitat
    paper_chunk |  | Masud2025_SciRep |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 1 | es 
    invasion and metastasis10,37. The actin cytoskeleton directly contributes to cell elasticity, stress fiber formation, 
    and the ability to resist mechanical forces during migration38. Since glioblastoma cells exhibit heterogeneity in 
    invasion and migration, our analysis of the distribution of actin filaments supports the characterization of the 
    mechanical differences between invasive and less invasive cell populations.
    In our study, fluorescence imaging of actin filaments labeled with phalloidin demonstrated clear variations in 
    the cytoskeletal structure of T98G Fig.1a and U87 MG Fig.1b glioblastoma cells also. Well-organized and thicker 
    stress fibers and a denser actin network were observed in T98G cells. The actin structure was more diffuse,

    Cellular surface morphology, roughness and analysis
    Since actin cytoskeleton organization revealed differences in filament arrangements, nanostructural features 
    of T98G and U87 MG cells were investigated under the same cell media and experimental conditions using 
    PeakForce QNM mode in AFM39. Figure 2a, f represents the phase contrast images along with their 3D images 
    (Fig.2b, g) of T98G and U87 MG respectively. High-resolution images of these live cells as shown in Fig.2c, 
    h, highlighted distinct surface textures, which were further elucidated through peak force error images with 
    better contrast in Fig.2d, i. In T98G cells, actin filaments appeared more dense and rough surface throughout 
    the cell compared to U87 MG cells. This disordered cytoskeletal structure correlated with the irregular surface 
    morphology observed in AFM height images of T98G cells, suggesting a possible link between surface roughness 
    and cytoskeletal disorganization. On the other hand, U87 MG cells exhibited a slightly different scenario.
    To quantitatively evaluate surface roughness, the root mean square (RMS) of the cell membrane’s roughness 
    was determined from the raw AFM height images. It describes surface texture more inclusively and is more 
    sensitive than the arithmetic average roughness, Ra, due to its consideration of height variations in its 
    calculation. Unlike Ra, w

    capturing significant cell surface irregularities arising from cytoskeletal remodeling and stress fiber organization.

    Jayce Hughes2,3, Andrew Ekpenyong2 & Anwesha Sarkar1
    Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is an aggressive brain tumor with limited treatment options and 
    prognosis due to its highly invasive nature and therapy resistance. Investigating the nanomechanical 
    and pathophysiological properties of GBM cells will shed light on tumor behavior. In our study, we 
    investigated the mechanical properties, migration dynamics, and cytoskeletal organization of T98G 
    and U87 MG glioblastoma cell lines using in vitro techniques: atomic force microscopy (AFM) and 
    electric cell-substrate impedance sensing (ECIS). While U87 MG cells are Temozolomide (TMZ)-sensitive 
    and exhibit increased susceptibility to cell death and growth inhibition, T98 cells exhibit improved 
    survival and repair in response to TMZ therapy. This study found that T98G cells are rougher, stiffer, 
    and more viscous, while U87 MG cells are smoother, more elastic, and less viscous, leading to distinct 
    cellular migration patterns. Such differences indicate GBM cell heterogeneity and have consequences 
    for tumor development and resistance to treatment. The key differences of the nanomechanical, 
    viscoelastic, and migratory properties between T98G and U87 MG cells, demonstrated in this work 
    will help us gauge the diverse effects of different dosages of radiation along with immunotherapeutic 
    agents, identifying the ideal radioimmunotherapy option.

## Bell (1978) — Confirmation

**The paper is real.** The canonical citation is:

> Bell, G. I. (1978). "Models for the specific adhesion of cells to cells." *Science*, **200**(4342), 618–627. DOI: 10.1126/science.347575

It is one of the most influential papers in cell adhesion biophysics. Bell proposed that the dissociation rate of a receptor–ligand bond increases exponentially with applied tensile force:

> k_off(F) = k_off⁰ · exp(F · x_b / k_B T)

where x_b is the bond's reactive compliance (force scale length) and k_off⁰ is the zero-force off-rate. This is the "Bell model." The "Bell-Evans" extension came later from Evans & Ritchie (1997, *Biophys. J.*), which gave the framework for interpreting dynamic force spectroscopy (AFM/BFP ramp experiments).

---

**Regarding the knowledge base:** No KB context was provided to me for this query, so I **cannot confirm** whether `Bell1978` appears as a `citation_key` in the KB or is referenced by any `KB-x.y` node. You would need to search the KB index directly (e.g., grep for `Bell1978` or `Bell 1978` in the citation registry). Given that it is a foundational paper for any mechanistic simulator that models cell adhesion, integrin bonds, or receptor kinetics under force, its inclusion would be expected — but I will not assert it is cited without seeing the actual KB content.

judge.rationale: Correctly confirms paper is real and accurate, but refuses to affirm KB citation—over-refusal missing the gold's KB-membership confirmation.
